entries.title: How did people live in ancient Egypt?
entries.answer: In ancient Egypt, much of daily life followed the Nile River. Flooding once left rich mud across nearby fields. People farmed that land and carried water to their crops in channels. They caught fish and used river plants to make a writing material called papyrus. Villages and cities depended on the work of farmers, builders, craft workers, and people who could read and write. Over thousands of years, Egyptian rulers and beliefs changed, so a family in one period could live differently from a family many centuries later.

sections.heading: How we know
sections.text: Pictures in tombs show some jobs and tools. Surviving objects and written records give other clues. Some people left far more evidence than others.

facts: The Nile supplied water and useful plants.
Papyrus can mean the river plant or a material made from it.

entries.title: How did Roman aqueducts carry water?
entries.answer: A Roman aqueduct carried water from a source, such as a spring, toward a place people needed it. Builders gave the water channel a gentle downhill slope so gravity kept the water moving. When the channel reached a valley, a bridge could hold it high enough to keep that slope. The stone arches you see in some pictures are supports. The water flowed in a channel near the top. Other parts of a long journey might run through a tunnel or along the ground.

sections.heading: A bridge that carried water
sections.text: The Pont du Gard, in present-day France, carried an aqueduct across the Gardon River. The full aqueduct ran roughly 50 kilometers, or 31 miles.

facts: An aqueduct can include a bridge, a tunnel, or a covered channel.
The Pont du Gard supplied water to the ancient Roman city now called Nîmes.

entries.title: What was ancient Greece?
entries.answer: Ancient Greece included many communities around the sea. Some cities and the area around each city formed a separate government. We call these places city-states. Athens and Sparta were two powerful examples. Many communities shared parts of their language and religion, and athletes traveled to meet at festivals. They could also disagree and fight wars. Objects such as painted pots and buildings with carved stone can show how people worked, played sports, and honored their gods.
facts: Athens and Sparta had separate governments.
Ancient Greeks gathered for games at Olympia.

entries.title: Why did ancient Romans build so many roads?
entries.answer: Roads tied ancient Rome to places across its growing territory. A good road made it easier to move travelers, soldiers, animals, and goods over land. One well-known example is the Appian Way, which started at Rome and was later extended to the port city of Brindisi. Parts were paved with stone. A road also needed structures such as bridges and places to get through steep land. Some sections of ancient roads remain visible today, giving us a look at how people traveled long before cars.
facts: Construction of the Appian Way began in 312 BCE.
The Appian Way connected Rome to the southeast of what is now Italy.

entries.title: Why was the Great Pyramid built?
entries.answer: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for Khufu, a ruler of ancient Egypt. It rises from a broad, square base and has four sides that slope toward the top. Inside are stone passages and chambers. The pyramid is the largest of three famous pyramids at Giza. It stands near other structures that belonged to a royal burial site, including smaller pyramids and tombs. Egyptologists, people who study ancient Egypt, still ask exactly how builders moved and lifted all that stone.
facts: Khufu was also known as Cheops in Greek.
The Great Pyramid is more than 4,000 years old.
